latin: Cūr ego graecam grammaticam ōderam<sup>1</sup>? Homērus mihi amārus erat.
Crēdō etiam graecīs puerīs Vergilium tālem esse, cum eum sīc discere cōguntur ut ego Homērum<sup>2</sup>.
Difficultās ēdiscendae<sup>3</sup> linguae peregrīnae quasi felle aspergēbat omnēs suāvitātēs graecās fābulōsārum nārrātiōnum.
Nūlla enim verba illa nōveram, et saevīs terrōribus ac poenīs, ut nōssem<sup>4</sup>, īnstābātur mihi vehementer.
Nam et latīnā aliquandō infāns utique<sup>5</sup> nūlla nōveram...
et tamen advertendō<sup>6</sup> didicī sine ūllō metū<sup>7</sup> atque cruciātū<sup>8</sup>...
inter blandīmenta<sup>9</sup> nūtrīcum<sup>10</sup> et joca arrīdentium<sup>11</sup> et laetitiās<sup>12</sup> allūdentium.
Hinc satis ēlūcet<sup>13</sup> majōrem habēre vim<sup>14</sup> ad discenda ista, līberam cūriōsitātem quam meticulōsam<sup>15</sup> necessitātem.
latinAccented: Cūr ego graecam grammáticam ṓderam<sup>1</sup>? Homḗrus mihi amā́rus erat.
Crēdō étiam graecīs púerīs Vergílium tālem esse, cum eum sīc díscere cōgúntur ut ego Homḗrum<sup>2</sup>.
Difficúltās ēdiscéndae<sup>3</sup> linguae peregrī́nae quasi felle aspergḗbat omnēs suāvitā́tēs graecās fābulōsā́rum nārrātiṓnum.
Nūlla enim verba illa nṓveram, et saevīs terrṓribus ac poenīs, ut nōssem<sup>4</sup>, īnstābā́tur mihi veheménter.
Nam et latī́nā aliquándō infāns útique<sup>5</sup> nūlla nṓveram...
et tamen adverténdō<sup>6</sup> dídicī sine ūllō metū<sup>7</sup> atque cruciā́tū<sup>8</sup>...
inter blandīménta<sup>9</sup> nūtrī́cum<sup>10</sup> et joca arrīdéntium<sup>11</sup> et laetítiās<sup>12</sup> allūdéntium.
Hinc satis ēlū́cet<sup>13</sup> majṓrem habḗre vim<sup>14</sup> ad discénda ista, lī́beram cūriōsitā́tem quam meticulṓsam<sup>15</sup> necessitā́tem.
english: Why did I hate Greek grammar? Homer was [bitter to me] (for me bitter).
I also believe [that] for Greek children Virgil [is the same] (such to be) when they are forced to learn him (thus... as) I [had to learn] Homer.
The difficulty of learning a foreign language thoroughly sprinkled, so to speak, with gall all the Greek sweetnesses of [those] fabulous tales.

[For I did not know a single one of those words] (none in effect those words I knew), and by cruel terrors and punishments, [they pressed me violently so that I should know them] (in order that I might know, it was pressed on me violently).
For [as for Latin words, I too] (and) [once, when] I was a baby, [certainly] knew none...
and yet, by observing, I learnt without any fear [and without] torment...
amid the caresses of the nurses and the jokes of those who smiled [at me] and [the] gaiety of my playmates.
From this it appears clearly enough [that] a free curiosity [has more power] (a greater force) for learning these things than a threatening necessity.

footnotes: You have already seen odi, odisti, odisse, a verb that only has the series of the perfect (like novi and memini). Oderam is a pluperfect: I had taken in hatred = I hated; it therefore has the sense of an imperfect.
Sic... ut..., just as... Both these words, which go in pairs, are sometimes separated, as here, sometimes joined in the word sicut, just as.

Ediscere = ex + discere: the prefix serves above all to insist on the force of the verb (idea of extraction). You will meet, on the other hand, the construction in the passive form seen in the previous lesson (N. 2), but this time the verbal adjective (ediscendus, -a, -um) is in the genitive. Fel, fellis, n., gall.

Nossem: short form of novissem, pluperfect subjunctive of novi. As novi has the sense of a present, the pluperfect therefore has the sense of an imperfect: that I might know (vid. sup. N. 1). Another example of a short form in the series of the perfect: amasti for amavisti, you loved; amassem for amavissem, that I had loved. Note the resemblance between French and the short forms. These forms are also found in Italian. For the moment do not try to use them, but simply note their existence. Do not, moreover, let yourself be impressed by these tenses that are new to you: we will come back to them in the next revision.
Utique, adv., entirely, certainly. Aliquando, sometimes, once.
Advertendo: ablative of the gerund of advertere, to observe; its compound animadvertere, to notice, is very commonly used.
Metus, -us, m., fear; metuo, -is, -ere, -ui, -utum, to fear.

Cruciatus, -us, m., torture, comes from cruciare, to torture; and the latter from crux, crucis, f., the gibbet, the cross. For the repertoire of insults: abi in malam crucem!, go and get yourself hanged! (go to the bad gibbet).
Blandior, -iris, -iri, -itus sum, to flatter, to cajole; whence the noun blandimentum (one also says blanditia).
Nutrix, -icis, f.: nouns in trix are feminine and correspond to masculines in tor. E.g.: spectator, spectator; spectatrix, female spectator.

Rideo, -es, -ere, risi, risum, to laugh; ludo, -is, -ere, lusi, lusum, to play. Arridens, -entis and alludens are the present participles of verbs derived from the two preceding ones. The prefix ad (transformed here into ar... and al...) adds the idea of going towards, in other words of laughing and playing, not by oneself, but in company.
Laetor, -aris, to rejoice. Laetus, -a, -um, joyful; whence laetitia, joy, gaiety.
Luceo, -es, -ere, luxi, v. i., to shine. Elucere = ex + lucere: idea of a light that bursts out, whence to appear clearly.
Vis, vis, f., force; acc. vim; abl. vi; irregular plural vires, virium.
Meticulosus, -a, -um (from metus, vid. sup. N. 7), fearful; méticuleux is a derived sense: he who is always afraid of not doing as he should, therefore careful.
comments: Alumnus, -i; f. alumna, -ae, the pupil (from alere, to nourish). — Vapulare: in spite of its active form, this verb has an entirely passive sense, since it is a question of receiving blows! Compare with our verb «to get a thrashing». You are getting a thrashing (in fact, «you are having yourself thrashed») will be vapulabis (future). — Discenda, nominative plural of the verbal adjective of discere, the things to be learnt. We could have said lectiones, the lessons, but this word would not have been appropriate. Lectio is indeed the lesson, but in the sense of actio legendi, the act of reading (e.g.: the reading of the manuscript, that is to say what one reads in the manuscript). So, when tomorrow you read «lectio quinquagesima tertia», remember that the lectio must be read and heard, whereas the annotationes are simply adeundae, to be gone [to see], to be consulted. Do not tire yourself pointlessly: today's lesson was rich in teaching. Tomorrow the lesson will be easier: you will be able to take advantage of it to go back over earlier lessons.

latin: Puerī mālunt lūdere quam scholam adīre.
Alumnī quī discenda nesciunt vel pēnsa male perficiunt, nōnnunquam vāpulant.
Sī in scholā lūserīs nec pēnsa perfēcerīs, rēctē vāpulābis.
Lūdendō tamen multa discuntur.
Puerī lūdentēs nōnnūlla ad artem hūmānam pertinentia discunt, praecipuē vītam commūnem, simul ac linguam suam.
Linguārum classicārum studium nōn est molestia taediōsa, sed lūdus jūcundus.
Hoc vērum nōn est nisi lūdendō discitur.
Cūr id fierī nōn possit?
latinAccented: Púerī mālunt lū́dere quam scholam adī́re.
Alúmnī quī discénda nésciunt vel pēnsa male perfíciunt, nōnnúnquam vā́pulant.
Sī in scholā lū́serīs nec pēnsa perfḗcerīs, rēctē vāpulā́bis.
Púerī lūdéntēs nōnnū́lla ad artem hūmā́nam pertinéntia discunt, praecípuē vītam commū́nem, simul ac linguam suam.
Linguā́rum classicā́rum stúdium nōn est moléstia taediṓsa, sed lūdus jūcúndus.
Hoc vērum nōn est nisi lūdéndō díscitur.
english: Children prefer playing to going to school.
Pupils who do not know their lessons or [who do their homework badly] sometimes [get punished] (receive corrections).
If you [play] (will have played) at school and you do not [do] (will have done) your homework, you will receive a correction, [and rightly so] (rightly).
However, by playing one learns many things.
Children [by] playing learn some notions relating to the craft of man, principally life [in common] (common), [and] at the same time their language.
The study of the classical languages is not a boring chore, but a pleasant pastime.
That is only true if one learns by playing.
Why could [that not] be done?

latin: Augustinus graecis pueris Vergilium amarum esse arbitrabatur.
Eum sic discere cogebantur ut pueri romani Homerum (discere cogebantur).
Augustinus nullum verbum linguae graecae noverat et tamen Homerum discere cogebatur.
Praeterea linguae, quam sermone communi non didicerat, grammaticam discere debebat.
Qua ex causa, puer, et grammaticam et linguam graecam oderat, adultus autem methodum pessimam fuisse intellexit.
Homerus poeta graecus erat, Vergilius poeta latinus.
english: Augustine thought [that] Virgil was bitter to Greek children.
They were obliged to learn him in the same way as Roman children (were forced to learn) Homer.
Augustine knew no word of the Greek language and yet he was obliged to learn Homer.
In addition, he had to learn the grammar of a language which he had not learnt through everyday conversation.
For this reason, [as a] child, he hated both the grammar and the Greek language, but [as an] adult, he understood that the method had been very bad.
Homer was a Greek poet, Virgil a Latin poet.
